name: Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents in the Second Half: A Survey
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2602.06052 [cs.CL]; cross-listed cs.AI). Submitted 2026-01-14 (v1); current v3 revised 2026-02-10. No peer-reviewed venue yet. NOTE: the task card listed the short title 'Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents: A Survey' and year 2025; the verified paper's full title includes 'in the Second Half' and its first arXiv submission is dated 2026-01-14, so year is recorded as 2026. The companion living paper-list repo is github.com/AgentMemoryWorld/Awesome-Agent-Memory.
authors_affiliation: Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang (co-first authors), Yueqing Liang and ~57 other authors; senior/supervisors include Philip S. Yu and Kai Shu (corresponding). 60 authors total. Primarily academic: University of Illinois Chicago (UIC), Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT), UIUC, UW-Madison, ASU, Emory, Northwestern, NTU, UCF, Rutgers, Cambridge, Harvard, UTokyo, UCSD, UCSC, TAMU, UCSB, MBZUAI, McGill, UCLA, Stanford; plus industry: Salesforce (AI Research), Google, Meta, Roblox, Cisco, Capital One.
code_url: N/A (a survey; no method code). Companion curated paper-list repository instead.
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/AgentMemoryWorld/Awesome-Agent-Memory ('Awesome-Agent-Memory', [Up-To-Date] paper resource; ~156 stars; last commit 2026-02-11; README mirrors the survey taxonomy: memory substrates, cognitive mechanisms, subjects, operations, learning policy, benchmarks).
task_domain: Survey/taxonomy of memory mechanisms for foundation (LLM-based) agents, spanning user-centric personalization/dialogue (conversation, recommendation, role-play, user simulation) and agent-centric task execution (QA/multi-hop, web/GUI, OS/desktop, tool/API, code/software engineering, embodied robotics/games, long video, scientific research) under long-horizon, dynamic, user-dependent environments. Anchor memory survey, not a single-task method.
problem_setting: A unifying survey arguing that as AI enters its 'second half' (problem definition + real-world utility over benchmark chasing), the central bottleneck is real utility in long-horizon, dynamic, user-dependent settings where agents face context explosion and must continuously accumulate, manage, and selectively reuse large volumes of information. It organizes foundation-agent memory along three orthogonal axes — (1) memory substrate (external vs internal), (2) cognitive mechanism (sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural), (3) memory subject (user-centric vs agent-centric) — then analyzes memory OPERATIONS under single- and multi-agent topologies, surveys LEARNING POLICIES over memory operations (prompting, fine-tuning, RL), discusses scaling (interaction horizon, environment complexity, environment quantity), and reviews evaluation metrics/benchmarks plus open challenges. Settings covered are predominantly interactive, long-context, single- and multi-agent; supervision varies by surveyed work. The survey proposes no new method, dataset, or experiments.
what_is_retrieved: Across surveyed systems: stored memory entries at multiple granularities — episodic interaction trajectories/events, semantic facts/concepts/entity-relations, procedural skills/workflows/reasoning patterns, user facts/preferences/persona, dialogue/session records, external documents/knowledge, and (for internal memory) parametric knowledge / latent hidden states / KV-cache. The survey frames retrieval as the 'Loading and Retrieval' memory operation that surfaces task-relevant memories for the current context.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID (survey-level). External memory is grounded in a GROWING/episodic agent-written store (vector index, text-record, structural store, hierarchical store) that the agent reads from and writes to, and may also wrap a STATIC external corpus (RAG over docs/KB). Internal memory (weights, latent-state, KV-cache) is parametric/transient. The survey explicitly distinguishes external (separated computation vs knowledge, scalable, editable) from internal (parametric, fast, hard to update) substrates, and argues effective systems use hybrid architectures.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Survey-level: the dominant surveyed retrieval objective is fixed top-k similarity (ANN over vector index), but the survey emphasizes balancing relevance, diversity, and context budget — too much retrieval injects noise/context overload, too little misses critical history. Graph/hierarchical routing (e.g., G-Memory neighborhood expansion into a core subgraph) targets a more complete experience set than flat top-k. It does not advocate a single completeness-vs-top-k objective; it treats retrieval quality (and the over-/under-retrieval trade-off) as a first-class design concern. [uncertain]
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (a survey, not a CBR method). However, the surveyed agent-centric experience-memory loop (store experience -> retrieve relevant episodes -> reuse/adapt at decision time -> revise/update memory) maps loosely onto CBR Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain, and the memory-operations framework (storage/index, loading/retrieval, updates/refresh, compression, forgetting) covers Retain/Revise dynamics. The survey does not use CBR phase terminology.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False — the survey is grounded in cognitive-psychology memory theory (Tulving episodic/semantic; sensory/working/procedural memory; Atkinson-Shiffrin-style multi-store analogies) rather than case-based reasoning; it does not frame itself as CBR and does not center Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.
retrieval_unit: Survey taxonomy of units rather than one: episodic events/interaction trajectories (sub-trajectory, action+feedback), semantic facts/concepts/entity-relations/KG-subgraphs, procedural skills/workflow-routines/reasoning patterns, user facts/preferences/persona records, dialogue/session segments, external documents, and (internal) parametric knowledge / latent hidden-state tokens / KV pairs. Retrieved 'reading' units are memory entries at these granularities organized in vector / text-record / relational-table / graph / tree / hierarchical stores.
index_source: Hybrid (survey-level). The retrievable store is mostly a GROWING memory written online during agent-environment/user interaction (indexed at write time with semantic embeddings + metadata: timestamps, task IDs, entities, tool usage), optionally combined with a STATIC external corpus (RAG). Internal substrates (weights via pre/post-training/editing/distillation; latent states; KV-cache) are induced parametrically/at inference. No single construction is prescribed; the survey contrasts external (online-grown, editable) vs internal (parametric) sources.
index_structure_topology: Survey-level: organizes external-memory stores into four substrate topologies — (1) flat vector index (HNSW/IVF/PQ ANN), (2) text-record (human-readable core summary + episodic/semantic lists), (3) structural store (relational tables via SQL / graph-based knowledge graph / tree-structured e.g. RAPTOR), and (4) hierarchical store (multi-store: core/episodic/semantic/procedural/resource/knowledge modules coordinated by a meta-memory manager). Multi-agent adds private-only / shared-workspace / hybrid / orchestrated memory layouts.
retriever_type: Survey-level (heterogeneous across works): predominantly dense embedding ANN retrieval over vector indices; plus BM25 / keyword / string match (text-record and hierarchical stores), symbolic SQL queries and graph traversal (structural stores), and LLM/agent-directed selection (memory-driven routing, meta-memory managers). Hybrid; no canonical retriever is proposed.
retriever_learning_signal: Survey-level spectrum, explicitly framed as a Memory Learning Policy along three paradigms: (1) Prompt-based (off-the-shelf retrieval + static/dynamic prompt-controlled selection, no training); (2) Fine-tuning (parameterized memory policies internalized into weights, retrieval refinement); (3) Reinforcement Learning (memory operations as a learned policy optimized by downstream task reward — step-level memory edits, trajectory-level compact-state learning, cross-episode/multi-agent). The survey highlights the shift from heuristic similarity to RL-optimized memory read/write/prune policies (e.g., Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MemAgent, MemSearcher).
query_construction: Survey-level: queries to memory are formed from current state/task (raw current query/sub-trajectory for similarity retrieval), with metadata pre-filtering (recency, task scope, memory type) before similarity ranking; agent- or LLM-generated structured queries (SQL, graph traversal); reflection/self-evaluation-conditioned retrieval; and state-matching against structured trajectory representations (e.g., SIT-graph episodic retrieval matches current execution state). Construction is method-dependent; abstracted as state-conditioned memory reading.
query_granularity: Survey-level: both task/session-level reads (recall user profile or relevant episodes at the start) and step/state-level reads during reasoning/acting (per-step retrieval in interactive agents, per-sub-trajectory matching). Multi-agent adds role-specific per-call memory views. No single granularity is standardized.
when_to_retrieve: Survey-level: spans one-shot (load relevant memory at task start), iterative/per-step (interactive agents read memory each step/turn), active (agent-/reflection-initiated reads, e.g., Talker-Reasoner deciding when to read; Self-Validator requesting more retrieval if evidence is insufficient), and adaptive (learned/RL memory-read policies, e.g., revisitable/look-back retrieval). No single trigger policy is prescribed.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Survey-level: triggers across works include fixed schedule (read each step/turn), metadata/loading filters (recency, task scope, memory type), agent-initiated/self-directed access, reflective/self-evaluative signals that trigger updating-and-refresh-and-read, orchestrator/controller routing decisions in multi-agent systems, and learned RL memory-read policies (reflective retrieval in Retroformer/Memento, revisitable memory in ReMemR1). The survey does not adopt token-confidence/attention triggers as a unifying signal.
reranking: Survey-level: after loading, memories are 'ranked or refined using semantic similarity, heuristic constraints, or budget-aware selection' before injection; multi-agent memory-driven routing performs explicit 'retrieval, scoring and reranking, selection' (e.g., S3 scores items by forgetting/relevance/source-credibility; G-Memory expands then compresses to a core subgraph then trims to role views). No single cross-encoder reranker is prescribed; reranking/scoring is treated as part of loading/retrieval and routing.
retrieved_context_refinement: Survey-level: refinement covered under operations — Compression and Summarization (condense episodic records into compact/abstract or hierarchical/tree representations; Dynamic Cheatsheets maintain a compact task-adaptive summary; ReSum/IterResearch summarization-based context management), Updates and Refresh (rewrite/merge/re-rank salient entries), and budget-aware selection/truncation to fit context. Distractor avoidance is discussed (over-retrieval injects noise; 'lost in the middle'). Refinement is a central operation, but no single post-retrieval module is prescribed.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (memory survey). Tool/skill-description engineering is largely out of scope, though procedural-memory skill/tool induction (e.g., TroVE verifiable toolboxes, ToolLibGen tool creation/aggregation) and resource-memory for documents/media are mentioned within the substrate taxonomy.
index_content_separation: Covered as a recurring pattern: hierarchical/virtual-context memory (MemGPT-style OS memory hierarchy) separates a small in-context working memory from a larger external store paged in on demand; text-record memory keeps a compact core summary indexing fuller episodic/semantic lists; hierarchical store uses a lightweight meta-memory-manager index routing to heavy per-module content; structural/tree stores keep node summaries+embeddings as a lightweight index over detailed leaves. Discussed as a substrate/management efficiency pattern, not a formal principle.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Partially: the survey notes MCP-based memory-source routing (Westhaeusser et al. orchestrator selects which memory sources to call via MCP and injects relevant snippets) and tool/API-centric agent benchmarks (AppWorld, tau-bench API invocation), but a static-vs-live tool index / CRUD auto-sync is not a focus of this memory-centric survey. [uncertain]
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (inter-tool dependency modeling is out of scope for this memory survey; procedural memory covers skill composition/sequencing but not tool-dependency graphs/bipartite KGs).
how_retrieved_used: Survey-level: retrieved memory is primarily used as prompt/context augmentation (inject recalled snippets/summaries/experiences into the LLM context for reasoning and decision-making); plus skill/workflow reuse (procedural memory invoked as routines), experience reuse for self-evolution and test-time learning (TTL without parameter updates), guideline reuse (CRMWeaver injects best-matching workflow guideline), and — for internal memory — implicit parametric recall (weights) or carried-forward latent states/KV-cache. RL-based policies also use memory as a learnable Markov state.
planning_integration: Survey-level: memory supports planning/acting by supplying relevant episodes/skills/state at plan and act time across agent topologies — single-agent per-step interleaved retrieval during reasoning; multi-agent orchestrated routing where a planner/controller selects which history to retrieve and inject at each step (MGA Planner, AgentFlow shared memory, LEGOMem task/subtask memory routing); shared experience pools queried by current sub-trajectory for in-context reuse (MAICC). The survey abstracts this as memory enabling long-horizon planning, skill reuse, and cross-session continuity rather than prescribing a single integration.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Survey-level: interleaving spans per-answer (one-shot recall then answer in QA), per-step/per-turn (interactive agents read/write memory each step), per-sub-trajectory (state-matching retrieval), and per-tool-call within rollouts (tool/API agents). RL trajectory-level work folds summarization/compression into the policy across multi-turn rollouts. No single granularity is imposed.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (a survey, not a CBR adaptation method). The closest analogues surveyed are Updates-and-Refresh (rewrite/merge/correct entries), Compression/Summarization (abstract episodes), and RL/fine-tuning policies that internalize or revise reused experience; for retrieved skills/guidelines, LLM-prompted reuse and execution-feedback-driven revision are described.
retrieved_item_representation: Survey-level: surface forms span raw episodic trajectories/event records, distilled semantic facts/concepts/entity-relations, free-text core summaries + episodic/semantic lists (text-record), executable/JSON-encoded procedural workflows/skills, structured KG nodes/edges and tree-node summaries, user-profile/preference records, and latent/parametric forms (weights, hidden-state 'memory tokens' as in MemGen, KV pairs). The survey explicitly contrasts non-parametric explicit memory with parametric/latent neural memory.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Survey-level spectrum: raw episodic interaction records -> distilled semantic facts/concepts (decontextualized from episodes) -> reusable procedural workflows/skills and abstracted strategies/reasoning patterns -> state-aware guidelines/rules. The survey explicitly describes an abstraction gradient: episodic experiences are 'semanticized' into stable semantic knowledge, and procedural memory evolves from explicit non-parametric templates toward implicit parametric neural policies.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Survey-level: discussed via the over-retrieval problem (excessive/low-quality memory injects noise and 'lost in the middle' degradation) addressed by budget-aware selection, summarization/compression, pruning/forgetting (recency decay, importance thresholds, learned removal e.g. BudgetMem/Mem-alpha), deduplication, write-control isolation (Memory-R1 ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP; WebCoach episode-completion writes), conflict resolution / consistency feedback loops (EvoMem constraint memory + verifier), and hallucination-oriented evaluation (HaluMem Memory Integrity / False Memory Rate). No single retriever-aware-training mechanism is prescribed by the survey itself.
memory_type: Survey/taxonomy — covers all listed types. By cognitive mechanism: sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural memory. By substrate: external (vector / text-record / structural-graph / hierarchical) and internal (parametric weights, latent-state, KV-cache). By subject: user-centric vs agent-centric. It does not pick one; it provides a three-axis taxonomy (substrate x cognitive mechanism x subject).
write_back: True (survey-level) — memory writing/storage-and-index is a core operation; agents store new experiences/facts/skills (indexed with embeddings + metadata at write time). Surveyed systems (Generative Agents, MemGPT, Mem0, A-Mem, Memory-R1, ReasoningBank, etc.) write back episodes/summaries/edits. The survey treats write-back, plus updates/refresh/compression/forgetting, as central operations rather than one implementation.
online_growth: Yes (survey-level) — external memory grows online during deployment/interaction (the survey's whole 'context explosion / scaling with interactions, environment complexity, environment quantity' framing); the store is written/updated across sessions. Internal parametric memory grows only via (costly) weight updates; latent/KV memory is transient per-session. The survey explicitly contrasts scalable online-growing external memory with hard-to-update internal memory.
write_back_trigger: Survey-level: triggers vary — per-step/per-turn writing, on-task-completion (WebCoach writes only after an episode completes; periodic/after-task summarization), reflective/self-evaluative writing (Reflexion/ReasoningBank store reflections), evaluation-signal- or conflict-triggered updates (rewrite when new evidence contradicts old), controlled write-time editing (Memory-R1 manager decides ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP), and human/system-validated writes (ChatGPT memory user control). The survey notes write strategy design (what/when to store) is vital but prescribes no single trigger.
failure_experience_usage: Survey-level: explicitly important — agents recall trajectories of previous failures and fixes to improve (e.g., coding agents recall failure trajectories to raise unit-test pass rates; cross-episode memory distills self-correction rules; EvoMem keeps a growing feedback memory of failures from earlier rounds; Reflexion/Retroformer store reflective/negative experience). The survey frames learning from both successful and failed experiences as central to agent-centric memory and self-evolution.
memory_evolution_update: Survey-level: covered under Updates-and-Refresh, Compression/Summarization, and Forgetting/Retention — beyond append-only, stored entries are mutated via rewrite/merge of overlapping episodic records, delta UPDATE/DELETE (Memory-R1), refine-overwrite of semantic summaries, importance re-ranking/refresh, dedup, recency-decay/importance-threshold forgetting, learned pruning, and graph link-and-evolve (e.g., temporal KG Zep, A-Mem entry linking). The survey stresses memory must 'evolve rather than merely accumulate' in non-stationary environments.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Yes (survey-level, highlighted) — Section 5 ('Memory Learning Policy') centers RL/learned memory policies: step-level memory-edit policies (Memory-R1 ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP, MemAct, MemAgent, RMM, Mem-alpha), trajectory-level compact memory-state learning (IterResearch, ReSum, MemSearcher, context-folding/summarization-as-policy), and cross-episode/multi-agent memory policies (Retroformer/Memento reflective retrieval, MAICC, SRMT). The survey explicitly contrasts these learned policies with fixed similarity top-k heuristics.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Yes (survey-level) — Section 4.2 dedicates the multi-agent setting: private-only vs shared-workspace vs hybrid vs orchestrated memory architectures; memory routing (orchestrator-based, agent-initiated, memory-driven); and isolation/conflict handling. Shared experience pools (MAICC, Spark, CRMWeaver shared guidelines), shared memory vectors (SRMT), hierarchical multi-agent memory (G-Memory), meta-memory managers (MIRIX), and collaborative/multi-user memory with access control (Collaborative Memory). Cross-framework sharing and 'agentic communities of practice' are surveyed and flagged as a key direction.
benchmarks: No new benchmark is introduced; the survey compiles two benchmark tables. User-centric (Table 3): MSC, DuLeMon, MemoryBank, PerLTQA, LoCoMo, DialSim, LOCCO, MemoryAgentBench, LongMemEval, HaluMem, PersonaMem, PrefEval, MemBench, MemoryBench, ConvoMem. Agent-centric (Table 4): HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, HLE, BrowseComp, Mind2Web, WebArena, WebShop, GAIA, OSWorld, AppWorld, tau-Bench, tau-Bench2, HumanEval, SWE-Bench, LoCoBench, LoCoBench-Agent, PaperBench, RECODE-H, ALFRED, ALFWorld, MineDojo, EgoSchema, Video-MME, LongVideoBench, MT-Mind2Web, MPR, StoryBench, Evo-Memory, LifelongAgentBench, OdysseyBench.
benchmark_family: memory (agent-memory evaluation survey) cross-cutting many families: QA / multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, HLE, MPR), memory/long-term-conversation (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, MemBench, HaluMem, PersonaMem, PrefEval, ConvoMem, MSC, DuLeMon, MemoryBank, PerLTQA, DialSim), web/GUI (Mind2Web, WebArena, WebShop, GAIA, BrowseComp, MT-Mind2Web), OS/desktop (OSWorld), tool/API (AppWorld, tau-Bench/tau-Bench2), code (HumanEval, SWE-Bench, LoCoBench/-Agent, PaperBench, RECODE-H), embodied (ALFRED, ALFWorld, MineDojo), long video (EgoSchema, Video-MME, LongVideoBench), and lifelong/test-time-learning agent (LifelongAgentBench, Evo-Memory, OdysseyBench, StoryBench).
baselines: N/A — a survey with no experiments. It tabulates and compares representative memory systems along its taxonomy (e.g., MemGPT, Mem0, MIRIX, A-Mem, Generative Agents, MemoryBank, Reflexion, Retroformer, ExpeL, Voyager, ARIGraph, RAPTOR, Titans, MEMORYLLM, HippoRAG, Zep, ReasoningBank, Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MemAgent, MemSearcher, G-Memory, AWM/Agent Workflow Memory, LEGOMem, MetaGPT, ChatDev, Collaborative Memory) rather than benchmarking baselines.
key_metrics: Survey-level metric taxonomy (Table 2) in three categories. Accuracy-based: Accuracy/Memory Accuracy, F1, Recall@K, MAP, NDCG@K, Success Rate (SR)/Goal Completion (GC), Pass@K/Resolved Rate (RR), Memory Integrity (MI), False Memory Rate (FMR). Similarity-based: ROUGE, BLEU, Distinct-n, BERTScore, FactScore, Perplexity. LLM-as-a-judge: Response Correctness, Faithfulness/Groundedness, Preference Following. Plus capacity/efficiency (MemBench).
headline_result: N/A (no empirical headline number; it is a survey). Headline contribution: a unified three-axis taxonomy of foundation-agent memory — substrate (external vs internal) x cognitive mechanism (sensory/working/episodic/semantic/procedural) x subject (user- vs agent-centric) — plus a memory-operations framework (storage/index, loading/retrieval, updates/refresh, compression/summarization, forgetting/retention; single- and multi-agent), a learning-policy taxonomy (prompting / fine-tuning / RL), and curated metric + benchmark tables, synthesizing 218 papers from 2023 Q1 to 2025 Q4.
ablations: N/A (no experiments/ablations). The survey's comparative benchmark tables (Table 3 user-centric memory abilities FE/MR/TR/UR/CS/FR/UP/AS/IC/AB coverage; Table 4 agent-centric env/interact/abilities) and the metric table function as structured cross-system comparisons clarifying which design choices and abilities each benchmark/system covers.
evaluation_decoupling: Yes (conceptually, a key argument). The survey repeatedly stresses making evaluation 'attributable to the memory mechanism' by separating retrieval/selection from generation: retrieval/ranking metrics (Recall@K, MAP, NDCG@K) assess whether the memory interface surfaces the right items, while integrity/hallucination metrics (Memory Integrity, False Memory Rate) and operation-level scoring (e.g., HaluMem, LongMemEval question-type categorization) expose memory failure modes separately from end-task accuracy. It explicitly calls for next-gen benchmarks to add memory-sensitive metrics beyond single end-to-end success.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both, as a taxonomy. Outcome: answer-level Accuracy/F1, SR/GC, Pass@K/RR. Process/intermediate: retrieval faithfulness/coverage, Recall@K/MAP/NDCG@K, Memory Integrity, False Memory Rate, Memory Retention Score, state-tracking error modes (drift/omission/contradiction), persistence under interruptions, and judge-based faithfulness/groundedness. The survey advocates complementing end-to-end success with memory-attributable process metrics.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Discussed qualitatively and as a metric dimension: external memory adds retrieval latency and storage/indexing cost that grows with horizon; internal/parametric memory is fast but costly to update; latent/KV memory scales linearly with sequence length. The survey calls for reporting computational/storage trade-offs (capacity & efficiency, e.g., MemBench; BudgetMem cost-efficient policies; efficiency trade-offs: memory size, update frequency, retrieval cost). No single quantitative speedup/cost number (it is a survey).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Survey-level: finite context window / 'context explosion' is the core motivation; memory externalizes state so agents do not retain all context in-prompt. Retrieval is typically top-k by similarity with budget-aware selection and reranked-then-truncated injection; fixed-size memory buffers under capacity constraints (MemAgent, BudgetMem) and adaptive forgetting/retention regulate budget. Benchmarks span max-context from ~1K to ~3M tokens (Table 3). No single budget/k value is prescribed.
survey_scope_and_axes: Organizing axes: (3) Taxonomy = Memory Substrates {external: vector index, text-record, structural store [relational/graph/tree], hierarchical store; internal: weights, latent-state, KV-cache} x Cognitive Mechanisms {sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural} x Subjects {user-centric, agent-centric}; (4) Memory Operations {storage/index, loading/retrieval, updates/refresh, compression/summarization, forgetting/retention} for single-agent, and multi-agent {architecture: private-only/shared-workspace/hybrid/orchestrated; routing: orchestrator-based/agent-initiated/memory-driven; isolation & conflicts}; (5) Learning Policy {prompt-based [static/dynamic], fine-tuning [parameterized policies], reinforcement learning [step/trajectory/cross-episode-multi-agent]}; (6) Scaling {interaction horizon, environment complexity, environment quantity}; (7) Evaluation {metrics: accuracy/similarity/LLM-judge; benchmarks: user- vs agent-centric}; (8) Applications; (9) Future Directions. Coverage: 218 key articles, 2023 Q1 to 2025 Q4 (curated from several hundred via Google Scholar + top-venue screening).
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A as a proposed benchmark (it is a survey), but it tabulates construction details for surveyed benchmarks: user-centric (Table 3) with #Sessions, #Questions, Max Tokens, data source Real/SIM/MIX, and ten memory-ability coverage flags (FE/MR/TR/UR/CS/FR/UP/AS/IC/AB) — e.g., LongMemEval 50K sessions / 500 Q / 1.5M tokens (MIX), LoCoMo 1K / 7,512 (MIX), ConvoMem 300 / 75,335 / 3M (SIM), MemBench 65K / 53K (MIX); agent-centric (Table 4) with #Data, Env, Interact, Resource (REAL/SIM/MIX), core abilities, and evaluation metric — e.g., SWE-Bench 2.3K (REAL, RR), WebArena 812 (SIM, SR), GAIA 466 (REAL).
builds_on: Cognitive-psychology memory theory (Tulving episodic/semantic memory; Atkinson-Shiffrin / sensory-working-long-term multi-store; procedural memory) as the organizing analogy; foundational LLM-agent memory systems it taxonomizes — Generative Agents, MemGPT/MemOS, Mem0, MIRIX, MemoryBank, RET-LLM, A-Mem, ARIGraph, Zep, RAPTOR, HippoRAG, Titans, MEMORYLLM; experience/self-evolving systems Reflexion, Retroformer, ExpeL, Voyager, ReasoningBank, Agent Workflow Memory; RL memory policies Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MemAgent, MemSearcher; multi-agent MetaGPT, ChatDev, G-Memory, LEGOMem, Collaborative Memory.
contrasts_with: Positions itself against prior memory surveys that used a single classification axis (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 'A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents' [sources/forms/operations]; Du et al. 'Rethinking Memory in AI: taxonomy, operations, topics'; human-inspired long-term-memory surveys) by adding the orthogonal three-axis view (substrate x cognitive mechanism x subject) and emphasizing learning policies and 'second-half' real-utility evaluation. Within the taxonomy it contrasts external vs internal substrates, user- vs agent-centric subjects, and heuristic vs learned (RL) memory policies.
lineage: Surveys group — a 2026 comprehensive memory survey for foundation agents. It builds on and extends earlier anchor memory surveys (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 LLM-agent memory survey; cognitive-architectures-for-language-agents) and sits alongside other 2025-2026 agent-memory/experience surveys, formalizing substrate/cognitive/subject axes, the memory-operation cycle, and the prompting/fine-tuning/RL learning-policy spectrum; downstream it frames the agent-memory research roadmap (continual/self-evolving agents, multi-human-agent organization, memory infrastructure/efficiency, lifelong personalization & trustworthy memory, multimodal/embodied/world-model agents, real-world benchmarking).
